topic.title: The festival we photograph is only the first ten days
topic.claim: We post the arrival, the lights and the pandal in full glory, and almost nobody posts the morning after, which tells you where our attention really sits.
topic.behaviour: Ganeshotsav photos of grand pandals and idols collect huge engagement online. The post showing the shoreline aftermath got far fewer upvotes than the pretty ones. Meanwhile mandals pick cheaper, easier-to-transport plaster-of-Paris idols and the clean-up becomes nobody's job.
topic.mechanism: Celebration is communal, visible and rewarded with likes. Clean-up is invisible and belongs to no one, and cost and convenience quietly decide the material of the idol. Everyone feels the festival is theirs, but the aftermath is someone else's.
topic.group: urban festival-goers and metro migrants in their 20s and 30s
real_details: A Mumbai user posted visarjan aftermath photos after sharing the pretty ones, and the commenters noticed it got far fewer upvotes than the Lalbaug-style posts
Commenters argued plaster-of-Paris idols are chosen because they are cheap and easier to make and transport, especially for very tall idols
One commenter recalled joining a school-club beach clean-up after visarjan about 10 to 12 years ago and never forgetting the sight
A Pune thread urged people to drop the unnecessary DJ and plastic excess during visarjan, and a commenter suggested home immersion of mud idols
A commenter said some idols belonged to well-known mandals, suggesting the issue isn't lack of money
topic.why_now: The photos are still circulating and the next big festival season is already here, so the pattern will repeat.

score.reason: Fresh angle on a familiar festival, backed by threads across two city subs, genuine guilt/belonging tension
score.best_hook: The pandal photo got 40,000 likes. The photo of the same spot the next morning, full of broken idols, got twelve. That tells you where we actually look.
